job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Karl Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in cost accounting at Brandt Pumps, a family-owned factory that makes industrial pumps, in Weldorf. I track what each pump costs to build, check the supplier prices and write a monthly variance report for the finance manager, Mr Lindqvist. I studied business administration with an accounting focus and finished top of my year, and I did internships at a car parts supplier and at my father's bakery's books. I rent a flat with a friend, Jonas, and my girlfriend Lena, a nurse, is there most weekends. On Saturday mornings I referee youth football, which keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I'd bet on, mostly noise. At work I'd say I use the tools a little for drafting emails and checking a formula, and that's the right size for them. I'd tell friends not to lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be pleased. A factory still has to buy steel, pay wages and ship pumps, and somebody who understands the numbers has to answer for them. I'd keep building experience and my pay would follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, finish the controller course the company is offering and ask for the variance report to be mine permanently. I'd save about £300 a month toward a flat deposit with Lena. I'd also help my father with his bakery's books at Christmas, when it's busiest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. Work is steady, the pay is fair for a graduate, and I like the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father's bakery. A new supermarket oven and a rent rise are squeezing him, and he's 58. I'd keep worrying about him, and I'd keep helping. That's not an AI issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it. The variance report is half manual lookups, and the assistant already speeds up the formulas. I'd expect Mr Lindqvist to ask me for more reports in the same time, not fewer people.

say: I'd say it's mostly **noise**, and the right size for a drafting tool.
I'd tell friends not to **lose sleep**.
I'd say the factory still needs someone who **answers** for the numbers.
think: I'm pleased, as numbers still need a **person** to answer for them.
The variance report is half **manual lookups** that tools speed up.
My father's **bakery** is my real worry.
do: Finish the **controller** course and own the variance report.
Save **£300 a month** towards a flat deposit with Lena.
Help my father with the bakery's **Christmas** books.
feel: **Content**, with steady work and fair pay.
S0.quote: A factory still has to buy steel, pay wages and ship pumps, and somebody who understands the numbers has to answer for them.
fieldNote: His calm stems from **steady** factory work and a fair wage.
His father's **bakery** is the main source of worry.
He expects **more tasks**, not fewer jobs, from small tools.

steps.text: Finish the company's controller course this year
Save £300 a month for a flat deposit with Lena
Do my father's bakery books at Christmas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's test it on one process and see if it's worth the money. I'd say we shouldn't throw out people who know how the factory really runs. Among friends I'd say it's what happens when a lot of paperwork piles up, and software finally copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my work changes a lot. The cost lookups and price checks are the sort of thing the software does cleanly. Mr Lindqvist told me the company will not hire for the finance team this year, and I read that as a sign. I'm not in danger today but I could be in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new system myself, early, and offer to run the test. I'd ask to take on the supplier negotiations, where a person has to look someone in the eye. I'd also pay down my student loan faster, since a lower fixed cost helps if things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense. I don't like being pushed, but I also know change is a part of work. I'd say tense and ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The price lookups and the first draft of the variance report. They take me a day each month and the software would do them in minutes. What I keep is checking why a pump cost more than expected, which needs me to walk to the shop floor and ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd keep the team the same size and ask us to do more. If two of us left, he'd likely not replace one. He's fair, but he answers to the owners, the Brandt family.

say: I'd say test it on **one process** first.
I'd say we shouldn't throw out people who know how the **factory** runs.
I'd tell friends software is finally coping with the **paperwork**.
think: My work changes a lot, with cost **lookups** being easy to automate.
I read the **hiring freeze** as a sign.
I could be in danger in **three years**.
do: Learn the new system early and **run the test**.
S1.quote: Mr Lindqvist told me the company will not hire for the finance team this year, and I read that as a sign.
fieldNote: Uses a **hiring freeze** as evidence, which is typical of his practical style.
He trusts his boss as **fair**, but notes the owners decide.

steps.text: Offer to run the company's test of the new costing software
Ask to take over supplier price negotiations
Put an extra £100 a month into the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the people in charge aren't doing their jobs if they let it land without a plan. At work I'd keep calm, but I'd say we should talk to the owners about what comes next. At home I'd say the family and the community have to hold together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be scared. If a machine does any desk job better and cheaper, a cost accountant is the sort of position that is gone in one budget meeting. I'm top of my class and it doesn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending, push savings to £500 a month and hold off on the flat deposit. I'd talk to my father about the bakery as a backup, because bread is something people buy even in a crisis, and I could do the books and the delivery side. And I'd keep refereeing, because I need something that's not about the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd feel it in the stomach and in sleep. I'd try to be steady for Lena and my father, but I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena and my parents that same weekend. My father would say come and help at the bakery if you need to, and Lena would say a nurse always has work. I'd feel guilty that she might become the main earner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the student loan at the minimum and put the rest into cash. I'd not buy the car I was thinking of. And I'd tell Mr Lindqvist I'm happy to learn anything if it means staying.

say: I'd say it's too fast and **leaders** aren't doing their jobs without a plan.
I'd tell the owners we need to talk about what comes **next**.
I'd say family and **community** have to hold together.
think: A cost accountant could be **gone** in one budget meeting.
Being top of my class **doesn't matter** here.
I'd feel guilty if **Lena** became the main earner.
do: Push savings to **£500 a month** and hold off on the flat.
Talk to my father about the **bakery** as a backup.
Tell Mr Lindqvist I'll **learn anything** to stay.
feel: **Heavy**, felt in the stomach and in sleep.
Trying to be **steady** for Lena and my father.
S2.quote: If a machine does any desk job better and cheaper, a cost accountant is the sort of position that is gone in one budget meeting.
fieldNote: His backup is **bread**: a trade people always buy.
Fears his own job is **expendable** whatever his marks.
Guilt over **Lena** earning more is a family-pride signal.

steps.text: Raise savings to £500 a month and delay the flat deposit
Skip the car purchase and cut eating out
Ask my father to take me on at the bakery if needed
Talk with Lena about whose job is safer and plan for it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair chance to prepare, and the owners at Brandt should start planning now. I'd say the company should train its own people instead of hiring strangers. In the football club I'd tell the older lads that the young ones need real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel better than at two years. By 2031 I'd be 27 and maybe a controller or in a team lead role, with a flat and a child on the way. Five years is enough to learn a trade properly twice, and I'd rather become an expert than a bystander.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the controller course and study part-time for a professional accountant qualification. I'd learn the AI tools as they come, but carefully. And I'd keep saving £350 a month toward the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady worry. I believe in work and effort, so I'd put my head down and get on. I'd not be happy, but not shaken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about the long game: a qualification, a flat, and a skill that suits a factory floor, like cost control in a plant where people need to walk the line. With two years I'd have no time for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Lindqvist sees it quietly. The older workers in the factory don't. My father thinks it's all talk, which I understand, but I'd warn him anyway.

say: I'd say five years is a fair chance, and the owners should **plan** now.
I'd say the company should **train its own** people.
I'd tell the older lads at football that the young need real **skills**.
think: I'd feel better than at two years, maybe a **controller** by 2031.
I'd rather become an **expert** than a bystander.
I'd put my head down and **get on**.
do: Finish the controller course and study for a **professional qualification**.
Learn the AI **tools** as they come, carefully.
Save **£350 a month** toward the flat.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to learn a trade properly twice, and I'd rather become an expert than a bystander.
fieldNote: He mixes **hard work** with planning, as his outlook suggests.
He would **warn** his father even though his father shrugs.

steps.text: Study part-time for a professional accountant qualification
Learn each new costing tool once colleagues use it
Save £350 a month for the flat
Warn my father and help him plan the bakery's future

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and we shouldn't make a fuss. I'd say employers should use the time to train people properly and keep apprenticeships going. And I'd say it's time governments stopped adding paperwork and let businesses get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel good. By 2036 I'd be 32, with a family, a flat, and maybe a senior finance role. I'd still worry a bit about what the next generation would do, but I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work up to controller, get my qualification, and then think about running finance at a small factory. I'd buy the flat with Lena and start a pension. And I'd offer to help my father to sell or hand on the bakery well, if he wants to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. I like having a plan that doesn't need luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade is enough to build a career and a family without having to hurry, so I'd start now and not wait for a crisis. With two years I'd have to panic. With ten I can just do the next right thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I'd like to be head of finance at a family firm like Brandt. What could stop me is the factory closing, a recession, or the finance function becoming a piece of software that needs nobody.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** and we shouldn't make a fuss.
I'd say employers should keep **apprenticeships** going.
I'd say governments should stop adding **paperwork**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 with a **family**, a flat and a senior role.
I'd still worry a bit about the **next generation**.
I like a plan that doesn't need **luck**.
do: Work up to **controller** and get my qualification.
Buy the **flat** with Lena and start a pension.
Help my father **hand on** the bakery well.
feel: **Settled**, since the plan doesn't need luck.
A touch of **concern** for the next generation.
S4.quote: A decade is enough to build a career and a family without having to hurry, so I'd start now and not wait for a crisis.
fieldNote: His fear is the factory's **closure** or a recession, which he calls the things a plan cannot control.

steps.text: Reach controller level and finish the professional qualification
Buy a flat with Lena and start a pension
Help my father plan how to hand on the bakery
Vote for parties that cut paperwork for small firms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I'm building takes a few years, and that scenario leaves me none. What would help is some warning from the company, apprenticeships and training kept going, and less red tape so small firms like my father's can survive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say I'm not frightened of work, I'm frightened of having no work to do. Give a person a fair chance to earn their living and most of them will use it well. That's all I ask.

headlineQuote: Give a person a fair chance to earn their living and most of them will use it well.
portrait: Karl is a **22-year-old** cost accountant at a family-owned pump factory, top of his class, with a girlfriend who is a nurse.
He uses AI tools now and then and adopts them once they're **proven**.
He is traditional and pro-work, so he trusts **apprenticeships**, family and effort, and dislikes red tape.
He is calm in slow worlds, **alarmed** at two years, and keeps his father's bakery as a fallback.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because his steady, step-by-step plans would have no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Warning** from employers, apprenticeships and training kept going, and less red tape for small firms.
